extracted.intended_audience: educators, school administrators, curriculum adopters, and educational researchers evaluating K–12 interventions
extracted.subtask_description: Applying What Works Clearinghouse (WWC) evidence standards to evaluate the effectiveness of a middle-school mathematics curriculum (The Expert Mathematician), including study inclusion, outcome measurement, and reporting of effect sizes and ratings.

rubrics_metrics.name: WWC rating categories
rubrics_metrics.description: "The WWC rates an intervention’s effects for a given outcome domain as positive, potentially positive, mixed, no discernible effects, potentially negative, or negative."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rating given for a domain (e.g., math achievement) must be one of these categories; see the WWC Intervention Rating Scheme for full descriptions. The report assigns the highest applicable rating given the evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors considered in rating effectiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: The rating of effectiveness takes into account four factors: the quality of the research design, the statistical significance of the findings, the size of the difference between participants in the intervention condition and the comparison condition, and the consistency in findings across studies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All four factors are considered together when assigning a rating; consult WWC technical documents for how each factor is operationalized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvement index
rubrics_metrics.description: The improvement index represents the difference between the percentile rank of the average student in the intervention condition versus the percentile rank of the average student in the comparison condition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The improvement index can take on values between -50 and +50, with positive numbers denoting favorable results. The WWC computes an improvement index for each finding and averages indices within domains and across studies. The improvement index is entirely based on effect size and does not depend on statistical significance or study design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion for 'Potentially positive effects'
rubrics_metrics.description: "Potentially positive effects: Evidence of a positive effect with no overriding contrary evidence."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit criteria: (1) At least one study showing a statistically significant or substantively important positive effect. (2) No studies showing a statistically significant or substantively important negative effect; fewer or the same number of indeterminate effects than showing statistically significant or substantively important positive effects. A single substantively important (though not statistically significant) positive finding can meet Criterion 1.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion for 'Positive effects'
rubrics_metrics.description: "Positive effects: Strong evidence of a positive effect with no overriding contrary evidence."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit criteria: (1) Two or more studies showing statistically significant positive effects, at least one of which met WWC evidence standards for a strong design. (2) No studies showing statistically significant or substantially important negative effects. If these are not met, 'positive effects' should not be assigned.

rubrics_metrics.name: WWC evidence standards and updates
rubrics_metrics.description: WWC evidence standards address methodological flaws such as non-equivalent groups at pretest and a mismatch between the unit of assignment and the unit of analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The WWC updates its evidence standards and applies peer-review procedures to adjust for flaws; these procedures were applied to the Baker (1997) study in this report. See WWC Tutorial on Mismatch and Technical Details of WWC-Conducted Computations for methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statistical corrections for clustering and multiple comparisons
rubrics_metrics.description: The level of statistical significance was reported by the study authors or, where necessary, calculated by the WWC to correct for clustering within classrooms or schools and for multiple comparisons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When appropriate the WWC will recalculate significance to account for clustering and multiple comparisons; in the Baker (1997) study no corrections were needed. See WWC Tutorial on Mismatch for explanations and formulas in Technical Details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study inclusion: meeting WWC evidence standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Studies included in the review must meet WWC evidence standards (e.g., randomized controlled trials or other designs that satisfy standards after adjustments).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Baker (1997), a randomized controlled trial, met WWC standards under both the original and updated reviews. The report only includes studies that meet the standards; absence of additional qualifying studies affects the strength of the rating.

rubrics_metrics.name: Required reporting of study characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Key study characteristics reported include: study citation, participants (demographics, N), setting, intervention description, comparison condition, primary outcomes and measurement, teacher training, and attrition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appendix A1 shows the format of required reporting. Providing these elements (e.g., sample size, randomization, number of classrooms/schools, and attrition) is necessary for WWC assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outcome measure reporting standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Outcome measures should be described (name, item count, content coverage) and psychometric properties reported (e.g., internal consistency/Cronbach’s alpha).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: The Objectives by Strand test is a 78-item multiple-choice test with 61 concepts and applications items and average internal consistency (Cronbach’s alpha) > 0.90; no norms were available. Report how/when the test was administered and by whom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling of pretest differences and attrition
rubrics_metrics.description: Pretest differences and attrition should be reported and handled; e.g., the pretest may be used as a covariate to control for post-attrition differences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In Baker (1997), differences in a math pretest favored the comparison group by 5.3 points; the pretest was used as a covariate in posttest analyses, and attrition rates were similar across groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect reporting elements (mean difference, SD, effect size, significance, improvement index)
rubrics_metrics.description: For each finding the WWC reports the study sample, sample size (schools/students), group means and standard deviations, mean difference (intervention - comparison), statistical significance, effect size, and improvement index.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appendix A3 provides a table with these elements; domain averages are also computed and rounded per WWC procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and interpretation of statistical significance and substantive importance
rubrics_metrics.description: Statistical significance is the probability that the difference between groups is a result of chance; the WWC also considers 'substantively important' effects (large enough effect sizes) even if not statistically significant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The WWC uses both significance and substantive importance when assigning ratings; e.g., a non-significant but substantively important effect can contribute to a 'potentially positive' rating.

rubrics_metrics.name: Domain averaging and calculation rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Within each outcome domain, the WWC computes an average improvement index for each study and an average improvement index across studies; the domain average effect size is a simple average.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Domain improvement indices are calculated from the average effect size. See Technical Details of WWC-Conducted Computations for formulas and rounding rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intervention implementation and fidelity reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Intervention descriptions should include curriculum content, lesson length and frequency, delivery mode (software + print), teacher preparation, and how intervention and comparison were administered (e.g., separate classrooms, same teachers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example details from The Expert Mathematician: 196 lessons teaching Logo, lessons 40–120 minutes, sessions every other day for one school year, students worked individually or in pairs using printed materials and computer; same teachers taught both conditions and no teacher training was reported. Such implementation details inform interpretation of effects.
